clusters.name: Consistency Model
clusters.description: This dimension distinguishes client-visible consistency requirements and the correctness consequences of choosing strong or eventual repository state.

relations.rationale: Strong client consistency constrains truth-formation designs to provide coordinated, durable ordering rather than exposing stale derived state.
Strong consistency constrains replica architectures toward coordinated state management instead of independently interchangeable replicas.

values.label: Strong consistency for Git clients
values.description: Repository operations expose coordinated, current state to Git clients.

values.label: Eventual-consistency repository design
values.description: Repository state may lag across locations, making it unsuitable for reliable Git client operations.

values.label: Stale repository state
values.description: Client-visible repository data can be outdated when consistency is eventual.

values.label: Unreliable repository operations
values.description: Eventual consistency can cause repository operations to behave unreliably for clients.

clusters.name: Truth Formation Strategy
clusters.description: This dimension distinguishes how repository truth is established, recorded, and derived, independently of replica topology or client-visible consistency requirements.

values.label: Consensus-before-action architecture
values.description: An operation proceeds only after consensus establishes the required state transition.

values.label: Log-first operation recording
values.description: Operations are durably recorded before repository state is derived from them.

values.label: Post hoc truth derivation
values.description: Repository truth is reconstructed or computed after operations have been recorded.

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead log
values.description: An S3-backed durable log records repository operations as the foundation for scalable repository state.

clusters.name: Replica Topology
clusters.description: This dimension distinguishes replica coordination, statefulness, minimum counts, interchangeability, and the operational cost of repository replicas.

values.label: Consensus-replicated repository architecture
values.description: Repository state is maintained across replicas through consensus coordination.

values.label: Consensus replication
values.description: Consensus replication is explicitly replaced by another durability and scaling approach.

values.label: Stateful repository replicas
values.description: Replicas retain substantial repository state rather than acting as stateless interchangeable workers.

values.label: Pet-style infrastructure
values.description: Replicas are individually managed, costly, and non-fungible infrastructure units.

values.label: Safe minimum replica count
values.description: The architecture maintains a minimum replica population needed for repository durability and correctness.

values.label: Replica non-interchangeability
values.description: Stateful repository replicas cannot be treated as equivalent replacement units.

values.label: Scaling complexity
values.description: Stateful, individually managed replicas make repository scaling more difficult.

values.label: Replica replacement complexity
values.description: Replacing replicas is more difficult when they retain unique repository state.

values.label: Maintenance burden
values.description: Individually managed stateful replicas increase ongoing maintenance work.

values.label: Higher repository operating cost
values.description: Consensus-replicated, stateful repositories impose higher operating costs than interchangeable replicas.

values.label: Replication cost for tiny repositories
values.description: Replicating very large numbers of small repositories creates substantial operational expense.

clusters.name: Consistency Model
clusters.description: This dimension distinguishes client-visible consistency guarantees and the correctness, reliability, and latency consequences of repository-state coordination.

relations.rationale: Strong consistency requires coordinated replica state and therefore constrains the available coordination strategies.
Consistency requirements constrain when repository changes become authoritative and how derived state may be exposed.

values.label: Strong consistency for Git clients
values.description: Repository operations expose coordinated, current state to Git clients.

values.label: Eventual-consistency repository design
values.description: Repository state may lag across locations, making it unsuitable for reliable Git client operations.

values.label: Stale repository state
values.description: Client-visible repository data can be outdated when consistency is eventual.

values.label: Unreliable repository operations
values.description: Eventual consistency can cause repository operations to behave unreliably for clients.

values.label: Consistency-and-correctness priority
values.description: The architecture explicitly prioritizes preserving consistency and correctness across replicas.

values.label: Higher tail write latency
values.description: Strong coordination produces increased tail write latency at scale.

values.label: Repository consistency improvement
values.description: Consensus-replicated repositories are intended to improve repository consistency.

values.label: Hosting reliability improvement
values.description: The architecture is intended to improve the reliability of repository hosting.

clusters.name: Replica Coordination Strategy
clusters.description: This dimension distinguishes how replicas coordinate agreement and whether operations require consensus before repository state changes proceed.

relations.rationale: Replica coordination choices determine the consistency guarantees and latency consequences visible to Git clients.

clusters.name: Repository Source-of-Truth Storage
clusters.description: This dimension distinguishes the storage substrate that holds repository objects or durable operation records and anchors repository truth.

relations.rationale: Storage substrates interact with whether repository state is derived from durable operation records or materialized through another process.

values.label: Filesystem-based repository storage

values.label: Distributed object-store repository hosting

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead log

values.label: Blob storage with relational database

values.label: Distributed key-value Git-object storage

clusters.name: State Derivation Strategy

clusters.name: Client-Server Responsibility
clusters.description: This dimension distinguishes whether repository scaling and virtualization responsibilities remain server-side or shift to Git clients.

relations.rationale: Shifting responsibility to clients reduces the need to redesign server-side repository storage.
Client-side virtualization changes the server replica and infrastructure requirements for repository access.

values.description: GVFS and Scalar virtualize repository access at the client rather than redesigning server-side storage.

values.label: Server-side repository-storage redesign
values.description: Redesigning server-side repository storage was considered as an alternative to client virtualization but not pursued.

values.label: Reduced local checkout cost
values.description: Client-side virtualization lowers the cost of local repository checkouts.

values.label: Client-server responsibility allocation
values.description: Architectures differ in whether repository-management and virtualization responsibilities reside in hosting infrastructure or clients.

uncovered_concepts: Blob storage combined with relational database
Distributed key-value store for Git objects
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers consistency, truth formation, and replica topology, including consensus, replication costs, and replica interchangeability. However, several relevant codes expose three additional architectural axes. First, the taxonomy does not capture where repository source of truth and Git objects reside—the storage substrate or placement axis distinguishing filesystem storage, distributed filesystems, object stores, key-value stores, and hybrid blob/database designs. Second, it does not capture where repository virtualization and scaling responsibility is allocated between clients and servers, as illustrated by GVFS/Scalar versus server-side storage redesigns. Third, it does not explicitly model the distribution of maintenance and compaction work across replicas. The CPU and bandwidth codes are consequences of that maintenance-placement choice. Other codes, such as consensus consistency, reliability, scalability, correctness, replica tradeoffs, and tail write latency, are outcomes or positions already subsumable under the existing consistency and replica-topology dimensions.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask different questions: consistency/coordination (1), storage substrate (2), replica lifecycle and maintenance (4), and client-versus-server responsibility (5) are generally separable. criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: Most dimensions are specific architectural axes, and there are no explicit labels such as 'Other' or 'Miscellaneous'. However, dimension 4, 'Replica Lifecycle and Operations', is a catch-all: its description bundles statefulness, individuality, population, replacement, scaling, placement of maintenance, and several unrelated outcomes. Reorganize dimension 4 by separating the existing replica-model values (4.1–4.3) from maintenance-placement values such as 4.4, using more focused dimension names rather than the broad 'Lifecycle and Operations' bucket.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy captures several relevant axes, especially storage substrate for GitHub's filesystem experiments and Google's object-store attempt, and client/server responsibility for GVFS/Scalar. However, dimension 1, "Replica Consistency and Coordination," combines two decisions—client-visible consistency guarantees and replica-agreement mechanisms—so it should be split into separate consistency and coordination dimensions, moving values 1.4–1.6 to the latter. Dimension 4, "Replica Lifecycle and Operations," bundles replica statefulness, replica population, and maintenance placement; reorganize 4.1–4.3 under a replica lifecycle/population question and remove or relocate 4.4, "Primary-only compaction," because it answers a separate maintenance-placement question. Value 3.3, "S3-backed write-ahead log," is a concrete storage/durability implementation rather than an answer to the state-derivation question; move it to the storage/source-of-truth dimension. These structural issues obscure the distinctions between Spokes consensus replication and Continuity/Origin's WAL-based approach.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: Dimensions 2, Repository Storage Substrate, and 5, Client-Server Responsibility Allocation, are coherent and each has at least two candidate decisions relevant to the filesystem/object-store and GVFS/Scalar alternatives. However, dimension 1, Replica Consistency and Coordination, mixes client-visible guarantees (1.1, 1.2), priorities (1.3), coordination mechanisms (1.4, 1.5), and historical replacement (1.6); split it into guarantee and coordination questions, moving 1.3 to the question it actually answers. Dimension 4, Replica Lifecycle and Operations, combines statefulness, pet infrastructure, replica count, and compaction placement; retain 4.1-4.3 under a clearly scoped replica-management question and move 4.4 to a maintenance/compaction decision point, or reorganize these values so each resulting question has at least two candidates. Dimension 3, Repository State Derivation, mostly addresses log-first versus post hoc derivation, but 3.3 is a specific S3 implementation rather than an alternative answer; merge it with the log-first value or move it to the storage-substrate decision. These mixed questions substantially weaken the requested orthogonal decision-point taxonomy despite the strong storage and responsibility dimensions.

criteria.name: Rejected-alternative handling
criteria.description: For each candidate decision, the taxonomy makes clear whether sources adopted it, rejected it, or disagree (status 'accepted', 'rejected' or 'mixed'); a rejected alternative is never presented as adopted; each candidate decision appears once with its stance; outcomes (status 'outcome') are kept apart from candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: Most values use valid statuses, and rejected candidates such as 1.2, 2.3, 2.4, and 5.2 are not described as adopted; outcomes are generally expressed as effects. However, dimension 1 duplicates the consensus-replication decision in 1.5 (accepted) and 1.6 (mixed); merge them and retain one status. The mixed descriptions for 1.6 and 2.5 state that the approaches were replaced or rejected, so revise them to acknowledge disagreement or use a non-mixed status. In dimension 5, outcome 5.4 is phrased as the alternative allocation decision itself rather than an effect; drop it or move/merge it with the candidate decisions 5.1 and 5.2.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Every sampled passage that discusses a design decision can be placed under at least one decision point (dimension) of the taxonomy.
criteria.reason: All decision-bearing passages can be placed under the taxonomy. The Git storage alternatives in d8c24866, 744b2d0b, and 71d49115 map to dimension 2; the Cursor WAL and state-derivation decisions in cc5ed95d and 948d9850 map to dimension 3; Spokes consistency, latency, and replica tradeoffs in 72d5f761, 18a2da1f, f4be69bf, and c247d568 map to dimensions 1 and 4; and Microsoft's client virtualization in 5edb9c3e maps to dimension 5. The lessons and evolution passages are likewise covered by the corresponding accepted values and outcomes. No coverage shortcoming was identified.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: No material shortcomings found. The taxonomy names the specific adopted and rejected options across the decision passages: S3-backed write-ahead logging (3.3), consensus and eventual consistency alternatives (1.1–1.6), filesystem, object-store, blob-plus-relational, distributed-filesystem, and distributed-key-value storage (2.1–2.5), primary-only compaction and minimum replica count (4.3–4.4), and client-side Git virtualization versus server redesign (5.1–5.2). The remaining passages are background, tradeoff, or outcome discussions whose concrete options are likewise represented.
